prompt: The introduction deck names which two types of register?

options.text: General-purpose registers and special-purpose registers such as the Program Counter and Stack Pointer

explanation: General-purpose and special-purpose, with the Program Counter and the Stack Pointer as the two named special ones.

why.a: Correct. General-purpose and special-purpose, with the Program Counter and the Stack Pointer as the two named special ones.
why.b: Wrong. The cache is a level of memory, not a class of register.
why.c: Wrong. Input and output are handled by I/O systems.
why.d: Wrong. Physical and logical describe addresses, not registers.

prompt: Registers are small, fast storage locations {{1}} the CPU.
explanation: Inside the CPU. That word is what separates a register from the cache, which is close to the processor but not within it.

prompt: Select the real-life applications of register sets the deck gives.

options.text: High-speed computation: programs execute faster when data is in registers instead of memory
Real-time systems such as air traffic control rely on fast register operations
Mobile devices: efficient register usage improves battery life and performance
Cloud systems: efficient register usage supports large-scale computing

explanation: Three applications. Cloud systems appear on the memory organization slide, not the register one.

why.a: Correct, high-speed computation heads the list.
why.b: Correct, with air traffic control as the named example.
why.c: Correct, mobile devices close the list.
why.d: Wrong. Cloud systems are listed under memory organization.

prompt: Computer organization deals with:

options.text: How architectural features are physically implemented

explanation: The physical implementation of architectural features. The other three options are all architectural components.

why.a: Correct. The physical implementation of architectural features.
why.b: Wrong. The instruction set is architectural.
why.c: Wrong. Data types and representation is architectural.

prompt: The first component of computer organization listed in the introduction deck is the {{1}} unit.
explanation: The control unit, and the ALU follows it. The revision class lists the same six components in the same order.

prompt: The control unit coordinates all operations of the CPU by doing what?
explanation: Fetch, decode, generate control signals. Arithmetic belongs to the ALU, which is the next organizational component.

why.c: Correct, generating control signals is third.
why.d: Wrong. Arithmetic and logic operations are the ALU's work.

prompt: Which component of the CPU coordinates all its operations?
explanation: The control unit, by fetching, decoding and generating control signals. Coordination is the word to look for.

why.a: Correct. The control unit, by fetching, decoding and generating control signals.
why.b: Wrong. The ALU computes; it does not coordinate.
why.d: Wrong. Buses carry data, addresses and control signals, but the signals come from the control unit.

topic: real-life applications of the control unit
prompt: Select the real-life applications of the control unit the deck gives.

options.text: Processor execution: every program relies on the control unit
Industrial automation: machines operate based on control signals
Robotics systems: it controls sensors and actuators
Digital calculators: they perform arithmetic operations

explanation: Three applications. Digital calculators are listed under the ALU, since arithmetic is what they do.

why.a: Correct, processor execution heads the list.
why.c: Correct, robotics systems close the list.
why.d: Wrong. Digital calculators appear under the arithmetic logic unit.

prompt: Select the operations the Arithmetic Logic Unit performs, according to the deck.
explanation: Two arithmetic operations and three logical ones. Fetching is the control unit's job.

why.a: Correct, addition is given as an arithmetic operation.
why.c: Correct, AND is a logical operation.
why.d: Correct, OR is a logical operation.
why.e: Correct, NOT closes the logical list here, though the ISA deck names exclusive-OR instead.
why.f: Wrong. Fetching instructions is done by the control unit.

prompt: The ALU performs {{1}} operations such as addition and subtraction, and {{2}} operations such as AND, OR and NOT.
explanation: Arithmetic and logical, which is where the unit's name comes from.

prompt: Which application does the deck list under the ALU, saying its neural network computations involve massive arithmetic operations?
explanation: Artificial intelligence systems, alongside digital calculators and gaming systems.

why.a: Correct. Artificial intelligence systems, alongside digital calculators and gaming systems.
why.b: Wrong. Robotics is listed under the control unit.
why.c: Wrong. Cloud systems are listed under memory organization.
why.d: Wrong. Smart homes are listed under I/O systems.

prompt: In the introduction deck's memory organization component, which level is described as fastest?
explanation: Cache is marked fastest on this slide, which lists cache, main memory and secondary storage. The memory deck's fuller table puts registers above cache.

why.b: Wrong. Main memory is the middle of the three named here.
why.c: Wrong. Secondary storage is the slowest of the three.
why.d: Wrong. Tertiary storage is not on this slide at all.

prompt: The introduction deck says memory is organized {{1}}: cache, main memory, secondary storage.
explanation: Hierarchically, which is the idea the memory deck then develops into a five-level table.

prompt: Which application does the deck attach to cache memory speeding up page loading?
explanation: Web browsers. Smartphones get the app performance reason and cloud systems get large-scale computing.

why.b: Wrong. Smartphones are named for faster app performance.
why.c: Wrong. Cloud systems are named for supporting large-scale computing.
why.d: Wrong. Gaming computers appear under system buses, for graphics performance.

prompt: Input/output systems handle:

options.text: Communication between the computer and external devices
Communication between the ALU and the registers
Translation of logical to physical addresses

explanation: The computer and the outside world. Everything internal belongs to some other component.

why.a: Correct. The computer and the outside world.
why.b: Wrong. That traffic is internal to the processor.
why.c: Wrong. Address translation is virtual memory's job, through the MMU.

prompt: Input/output systems handle communication between the computer and {{1}} devices.
explanation: External devices, which is why keyboards, monitors and sensors are its examples.

prompt: Match each real-life application of I/O systems to the deck's description.

pairs.right: Sensors provide input, displays provide output

explanation: Three applications, and each names an input and an output, which is the point of the component.

prompt: Select the three types of bus the deck names.
explanation: Data, address, control. They match exactly what buses transfer: data, addresses and control signals.

why.a: Correct, the data bus carries the data.
why.b: Correct, the address bus carries the addresses.
why.c: Correct, the control bus carries the control signals.
why.d: Wrong. There is no instruction bus here; instructions travel on the data bus. A separate instruction path is the Harvard architecture, a different idea.

prompt: Buses transfer data, {{1}} and {{2}} signals.
explanation: Data, addresses, control signals, which is why there are exactly three buses.

prompt: In the real-life applications of system buses, which system does the deck say uses high-speed buses to improve graphics performance?
explanation: Gaming computers. Servers get efficient data transfer supporting multiple users, and motherboard communication heads the list.

why.b: Wrong. Servers are named for supporting multiple users.
why.c: Wrong. Smartphones appear under memory organization.
why.d: Wrong. Medical devices appear under I/O systems.

prompt: How does the introduction deck distinguish pipelining from parallelism?

options.text: Pipelining is overlapping instruction execution, parallelism is executing multiple tasks simultaneously
Pipelining is executing multiple tasks simultaneously, parallelism is overlapping instruction execution
They are two words for the same technique
Pipelining applies to memory, parallelism to the processor

explanation: Overlapping against simultaneous. Pipelining shares one datapath among instructions at different stages; parallelism uses more than one unit at once.

why.c: Wrong. The deck defines them separately on the same line.

prompt: Pipelining is the {{1}} of instruction execution.
explanation: Overlapping, which is the same word the pipelining deck uses throughout.

topic: real-life applications of pipelining and parallelism
prompt: Select the real-life applications of pipelining and parallelism the deck gives.

options.text: Modern CPUs execute multiple instructions at once
AI and big data systems handle massive computations efficiently
Web browsers cache pages to load faster

explanation: Three applications. Web browser caching belongs to memory organization.

why.a: Correct, modern CPUs head the list.
why.c: Correct, AI and big data systems close it.
why.d: Wrong. That is listed under memory organization.
